question: A shop's quarterly sales (₹ lakh): Q1 = 40, Q2 = 52, Q3 = 48, Q4 = 60. Between which two consecutive quarters was the percentage growth the highest?
d: Both Q1 to Q2 and Q3 to Q4, since each rose by ₹12 lakh
why: Q1 to Q2 is 12/40 = 30%, Q3 to Q4 is 12/48 = 25%. The rupee rise is equal but the base differs.

question: Four bus routes: R1 has 120 seats with 90 passengers, R2 has 80 seats with 66 passengers, R3 has 150 seats with 105 passengers, R4 has 60 seats with 48 passengers. Which route has the highest percentage of seats occupied?
why: Occupancy: R1 75%, R2 82.5%, R3 70%, R4 80%. R3 carries the most people but has the lowest share.

question: Daily units sold, Monday to Thursday. Store X: 120, 150, 90, 140. Store Y: 100, 130, 110, 170. By what percentage does Y's four-day total exceed X's four-day total?
why: X totals 500 and Y totals 510. The excess is 10 on a base of 500 (X), so 2%.

question: Three sections took a test. Section A: 30 students, average 62. Section B: 20 students, average 70. Section C: 50 students, average 58. What is the average over all 100 students?
why: Weighted mean = (30×62 + 20×70 + 50×58)/100 = 6160/100 = 61.6. The simple mean of 62, 70 and 58 is 63.33, which is the trap.

question: Revenue = price × units. Compared with the previous year, price changed by +20% in 2022, −10% in 2023 and +25% in 2024; units sold changed by −10% in 2022, +30% in 2023 and −20% in 2024. Revenue in 2021 was ₹50 lakh. What was the revenue in 2024?

Four towns (population in lakh; share of males; male literacy; female literacy): P (10; 55%; 80%; 60%), Q (8; 50%; 90%; 70%), R (12; 60%; 75%; 50%), S (6; 52%; 85%; 80%). Which town has the highest overall literacy rate?
why: Overall rate = male share × male literacy + female share × female literacy: P 71%, Q 80%, R 65%, S 82.6%. Q has the best male literacy but S wins overall.

question: Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north, in positions 1 to 5 from the left. Conditions: C is somewhere to the left of E; E is immediately to the left of A; A is immediately to the left of B; C and E are not next to each other. Who sits in the middle (position 3)?
why: Placing the conditions gives the order C D E A B from the left, so E is in the middle.

question: Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north, in positions 1 to 5 from the left. Conditions: A and C are not next to each other; D is immediately to the left of E; exactly 2 people sit between C and E; C is somewhere to the left of D. Who sits at the extreme right (position 5)?
why: The order from the left is C B D E A, so A is at the extreme right.

question: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. Conditions: A sits opposite C; D and E are not neighbours; D sits immediately to the left of C; A and B are not neighbours. Who sits opposite B?
why: Placing the conditions gives the clockwise order A E B C D F, so F is opposite B.

question: Six people P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row, positions 1 to 6 from the left. Conditions: U is somewhere to the left of Q; T is immediately to the left of Q; exactly 2 people sit between S and T; R is somewhere to the left of U; exactly 1 person sits between R and U. Who sits in position 4 from the left?
why: The row from the left is R S U P T Q, so P is fourth.

question: Eight friends A to H live on different floors of an eight-floor building, the ground floor being floor 1 and the top floor being floor 8. Conditions: G is somewhere below H; C and H are not on adjacent floors; C is immediately below D; H is somewhere below D; G is immediately below F; F is immediately below E; B is somewhere below F. Who lives on floor 5?
why: The floors from the ground upwards are B G F E H A C D, so floor 5 is H.

question: Eight friends A to H sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. Conditions: C sits opposite D; B and F are not neighbours; C and E are not neighbours; F sits second to the left of D; G sits second to the left of C; B and D are not neighbours; H sits second to the left of A. Who sits second to the left of G?
why: Placing the conditions gives the clockwise order A F H C B G E D. Facing the centre, left is clockwise, so second to the left of G is D.

question: Four boxes P, Q, R and S hold 28 balls in all. P has 2 more balls than Q. Q has 1 fewer ball than R. R has twice as many balls as S. How many balls are in P?
why: Let S = s: R = 2s, Q = 2s − 1, P = 2s + 1. The total 7s = 28 gives s = 4, so P = 9.

question: Asha, Bala and Chitra bought apples, mangoes and bananas (number of fruits). Row totals: Asha 15, Bala 12, Chitra 18. Column totals: apples 14, mangoes 16, bananas 15. Known: Asha bought 5 apples and 6 mangoes; Bala bought 4 apples and 3 bananas. How many bananas did Chitra buy?
why: Asha's bananas = 4, Bala's mangoes = 5. Chitra's bananas = 15 − 4 − 3 = 8, and her total checks: 5 + 5 + 8 = 18.

question: Six players A to F each scored a different value from 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 in a game. Clues: C scored exactly 20 more than D; F scored 20; B scored exactly 20 more than E; E scored 10. How many did A score?
why: B = 30 and F = 20 follow from the clues, leaving 40, 50 and 60. C is exactly 20 more than D, which only works as C = 60 and D = 40, so A = 50.

question: A trader sells three products in three cities (units). Row totals: Pune 14, Surat 16, Indore 15. Column totals: shirts 13, caps 17, belts 15. Known cells: Pune-shirts 3, Pune-belts 5, Surat-shirts 5, Indore-caps 4. How many caps were sold in Surat?
why: Pune-caps = 14 − 3 − 5 = 6. Surat-caps and Surat-belts add to 16 − 5 = 11, and caps total 17 gives Indore-caps 4, so Surat-caps = 17 − 6 − 4 = 7.

question: A 4×4 grid is filled with the digits 1 to 4 so that every row and every column has each digit exactly once. Given: Row 1: _ _ _ _ | Row 2: _ 1 _ _ | Row 3: _ _ 2 3 | Row 4: _ _ 3 _. Also, the entry in row 4, column 1 is larger than the entry in row 4, column 2; the entry in row 3, column 2 is larger than the entry in row 3, column 3. What is the entry in row 1, column 4?
why: Fill forced cells first using the row and column rule, then use the two inequality clues to settle the remaining choice. The grid has exactly one completion.

question: Ten identical laddoos are given to four children Anu, Binu, Charu and Dev. Each child gets at least 1 laddoo, Anu gets at most 3, and Dev gets more laddoos than Binu. In how many ways can this be done?
why: Fix Anu = 1, 2 or 3, then count the splits of the rest among Binu, Charu and Dev (each at least 1) with Dev > Binu. Adding the three cases gives the total.

question: In a knockout tournament, a team that loses a match is out. There are 13 teams. How many matches are played in all to decide the champion?
why: Every match removes exactly one team, and 12 teams must be removed to leave one champion, so 12 matches.

question: Seven teams play a league in which every team plays every other team twice (once at home, once away). How many matches are played in all?
why: Pairs of teams = 7×6/2 = 21, and each pair meets twice, so 42.

question: Five teams A, B, C, D and E play a league in which each pair meets once. A win earns 2 points, a draw 1 point each and a loss 0. At the end A has 7 points, B has 6, C has 4 and D has 2. How many points does E have?
why: There are 10 matches and every match hands out 2 points in total, so 20 points. E = 20 − (7 + 6 + 4 + 2) = 1.

question: Six players A to F play a chess round-robin: each pair plays one game, a win scores 1 point, a draw 0.5 each and a loss 0. Final scores: A 4, B 3.5, C 3, D 2.5, E 1.5. What did F score?
why: 15 games give 15 points in all. F = 15 − (4 + 3.5 + 3 + 2.5 + 1.5) = 0.5.

question: Five teams A, B, C, D and E play a round-robin: each pair plays once and there are no draws. Final wins: A 3, B 2, C 2, D 2, E 1. Further known results: A beat D; E beat B; C beat D. Which team beat A?
why: Using the wins column and the known results, all 10 matches are forced; the only team that beat A is B.

question: Six teams A to F play a round-robin: each pair plays once and there are no draws. Final wins: A 4, B 3, C 3, D 2, E 2, F 1. Further known results: C beat F; A beat B; C beat E; C beat B; A beat E; A beat F. Which team beat A?
why: A won 4 of its 5 games, so it lost exactly one. Combining the win counts with the known results fixes every match, and the only team that beat A is D.

question: Roads between towns (km): A–B 7, A–C 4, B–D 5, C–D 9, C–E 12, D–E 3, B–E 11. All roads are two-way. What is the shortest distance from A to E?
why: A–B–D–E = 7 + 5 + 3 = 15 km. A–C–D–E and A–C–E are both 16 km.

question: One-way roads: A→B, A→C, B→C, B→D, C→D, C→E, D→E. How many different routes lead from A to E?
why: Count routes by last stop: routes to E = routes to C + routes to D. Routes to B = 1, to C = 2, to D = routes(B)+routes(C) = 3, so E = 2 + 3 = 5.

question: Two-way roads (km): P–Q 6, P–R 11, Q–R 4, Q–S 8, R–S 6, R–T 10, S–T 3, Q–T 14. A courier must go from P to T and must pass through R on the way. What is the shortest possible distance?
why: Best route through R: P–Q–R–S–T = 6 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 19 km. The unconstrained shortest route, P–Q–S–T (17 km), skips R.

question: A metro has three lines. Red: P, Q, R, S, T. Blue: U, R, V, W. Green: X, T, W, Y. Lines meet at stations they share (R is on Red and Blue, T on Red and Green, W on Blue and Green). What is the minimum number of train changes needed to travel from P to Y?
why: P is on Red only and Y on Green only. Red meets Green directly at T, so one change at T is enough.

question: Two-way roads, each shown as (distance in km, toll in ₹): H–A (10, 40), H–B (15, 10), A–C (12, 30), B–C (25, 5), B–D (20, 20), C–D (8, 0), A–D (30, 10). A truck goes from H to D without visiting any town twice, and the total distance must be at most 40 km. What is the lowest total toll it can pay?
why: Routes within 40 km: H–A–C–D (30 km, ₹70), H–B–D (35 km, ₹30) and H–A–D (40 km, ₹50). The cheapest route overall, H–B–C–D (₹15), is 48 km, so it is too long.

question: A city has three train lines. Line 1: station 1 to 2 takes 6 min, 2 to 3 takes 10 min, 3 to 4 takes 12 min. Line 2: station 2 to 5 takes 5 min, 5 to 4 takes 9 min. Line 3: station 1 to 5 takes 12 min. Every change of line costs 5 minutes of waiting. All lines run both ways. What is the shortest time from station 1 to station 4?
why: Line 1 all the way takes 28. Line 3 to station 5 then Line 2 takes 12 + 5 + 9 = 26. Line 1 to station 2, change, then Line 2 takes 6 + 5 + 5 + 9 = 25. Forgetting the 5-minute wait gives 20.

question: A technician starts at 9:00 am. Task A takes 40 min, then Task B takes 25 min, then he takes a 15-minute break, then Task C takes 55 min and Task D takes 30 min. At what time does he finish?

Rohit is free 9:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00. Sana is free 10:00–12:00 and 13:00–16:00. Tej is free 10:30–13:30 and 15:00–18:00. They need a one-hour meeting at a time when all three are free. What is the earliest start time?
why: Common time: 10:30–11:00 (only 30 min) and 15:00–16:00 (60 min). So the earliest one-hour slot starts at 15:00.

question: A bank has two counters. Customers join one common queue in order of arrival and go to whichever counter is free (counter 1 if both are free). Arrival time (minutes after opening) and service time: C1 (0, 6), C2 (1, 8), C3 (2, 4), C4 (3, 5), C5 (4, 3). At what minute does the last customer finish?
why: C1 uses counter 1 (0–6) and C2 counter 2 (1–9). C3 gets counter 1 (6–10). C4 gets counter 2 (9–14). C5 gets counter 1 (10–13). The last finish is at minute 14.

question: Five exams (Chemistry, English, History, Maths, Physics) are held on five consecutive days, Monday to Friday, one per day. Conditions: Physics is on the day immediately before English; History is on an earlier day than English; exactly 2 days separate Chemistry and Physics; Chemistry is on the day immediately before History. Which exam is on Wednesday?
why: The conditions fix the order Chemistry → History → Maths → Physics → English from Monday to Friday, so Wednesday has Maths.

question: Two workers must finish six jobs; a job cannot be split and a worker does one job at a time. Durations (hours) and what must finish first: A 3 (none), B 2 (after A), C 4 (none), D 2 (after B and C), E 3 (after A), F 2 (after D and E). What is the least time in which all six jobs can be finished?
why: The chain A → B → D → F takes 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 hours and cannot be shortened. Total work is 16 hours, which would give 8 on two workers, but the chain forces 9 and 9 is achievable.

question: Seven candidates Arjun, Bhavna, Chetan, Divya, Esha, Farhan and Gauri are interviewed one per day on seven consecutive days, Monday to Sunday. Conditions: Gauri is on the day immediately before Divya; Esha is on an earlier day than Gauri; Divya is on the day immediately before Chetan; Chetan is on the day immediately before Bhavna; Arjun and Esha are not on consecutive days; exactly 1 day separates Arjun and Divya. Who is interviewed on Friday?
why: The conditions fix the order Esha → Farhan → Arjun → Gauri → Divya → Chetan → Bhavna from Monday to Sunday, so Friday is Divya.

question: In a class of 120 students, 70 play cricket, 55 play football and 20 play both. How many play neither game?
why: Cricket or football = 70 + 55 − 20 = 105. Neither = 120 − 105 = 15.

question: Of 200 people surveyed, 120 drink tea, 90 drink coffee and 40 drink both. How many drink exactly one of the two?
why: Only tea = 120 − 40 = 80 and only coffee = 90 − 40 = 50, so exactly one = 130.

question: In a group of 100 people, 60 like A, 50 like B and 40 like C. 25 like both A and B, 15 like both B and C, 20 like both A and C, and 10 like all three. How many like exactly two of the three?
why: The pair counts (25, 15, 20) each include the 10 who like all three. Exactly two = (25 + 15 + 20) − 3×10 = 30.

question: In a group of 100 people, 70 own a bike, 80 own a phone and 90 own a laptop. What is the minimum possible number of people who own all three?
why: People missing at least one item: at most 30 + 20 + 10 = 60. So at least 100 − 60 = 40 own all three.

question: A store has 110 customers. 70 bought X, 55 bought Y and 45 bought Z. 10 bought all three. 25 bought both X and Y (including those who bought all three) and 20 bought both Y and Z (including those who bought all three). How many bought only Y?
why: Y buyers = only Y + (XY only) + (YZ only) + all three. XY only = 25 − 10 = 15 and YZ only = 20 − 10 = 10. So only Y = 55 − 15 − 10 − 10 = 20.

question: In a town of 800 people, 60% read newspaper A, 50% read B and 40% read C. 30% read both A and B, 20% read both B and C, 25% read both A and C, and 10% read all three. How many people read exactly one of the three newspapers?
why: By inclusion–exclusion the readers of at least one paper are 60 + 50 + 40 − 30 − 20 − 25 + 10 = 85%. Readers of at least two are 75 − 2×10 = 55%. Exactly one = 85 − 55 = 30% of 800 = 240.

question: A father is 4 times as old as his son. After 6 years he will be 3 times as old as the son. What is the father's present age?
why: Let the son be s: 4s + 6 = 3(s + 6), so s = 12 and the father is 48.

question: Car A runs 15 km per litre of petrol costing ₹100 per litre. Car B runs 25 km per kg of CNG costing ₹80 per kg. How much less does Car B cost for a 300 km trip?

Mobile plan X costs ₹300 a month and includes 60 minutes; extra minutes cost ₹2.50 each. Plan Y costs ₹100 a month plus ₹3 per minute for every minute used. For how many minutes of use in a month do both plans cost the same? (Use more than 60 minutes.)
Raju spends 40% of his salary on rent, then 25% of what remains on food, then 20% of what remains after that on travel. He saves the rest, which is ₹21,600. What is his salary?
why: After rent 60% is left, after food 75% of that, after travel 80% of that: 0.6 × 0.75 × 0.8 = 0.36 of the salary. 21,600 / 0.36 = ₹60,000.

question: Income tax per year (₹ lakh): nil up to 3, 5% on the part from 3 to 7, 10% on the part from 7 to 10, and 20% on the part above 10. A person pays ₹1.6 lakh in tax. What is the person's income?
why: Tax up to 10 lakh = 0.05×4 + 0.10×3 = 0.5 lakh. The remaining 1.1 lakh is at 20%, so 5.5 lakh above 10. Income = 15.5 lakh.

question: Ajay invests ₹50,000 for the whole year but withdraws ₹10,000 after 8 months. Bela invests ₹40,000 and adds ₹20,000 after 5 months. At the end of the year the profit is ₹59,000. What is Ajay's share?
